common_name: HayDay Golden Bicolor Helenium (Fleuroselect Gold Medal Compact Sneezeweed)

planting.note: Plant rooted divisions or nursery starts in spring once soil has warmed, since this series is propagated vegetatively rather than from seed.

directions: Plant young HayDay Golden Bicolor starts in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing them around a foot and a half apart to let the dense, upright clumps fill in. This Fleuroselect Gold Medal-winning sneezeweed is bred for an unusually compact, well-branched habit compared to older seed-grown Helenium, carrying gold-and-copper bicolor daisies from late summer into autumn. Deadhead lightly to tidy the display, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring to keep flowering strong. Its dense branching makes it a reliable late-season nectar source for bees and butterflies.

common_name: Lemon Cutie Sunflower (Fleuroselect Gold Medal Dwarf Semi-Double Sunflower)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed, since sunflowers resent root disturbance from transplanting.

directions: Sow seed directly in full sun after frost danger has passed, thinning seedlings to roughly a foot apart since this dwarf sunflower branches freely at every leaf joint rather than growing a single stalk. Lemon Cutie was the first dwarf, semi-double, branching sunflower bred without pollen, opening a ring of slender lemon-yellow petals around a denser central cluster of rolled petals on a plant that tops out under two feet. Because it keeps producing smaller flushes of flowers through summer into fall, it suits containers and small beds better than tall single-stem sunflower types. Its lack of pollen also makes it a tidier choice for cutting and for gardeners sensitive to sunflower pollen.

common_name: Goldblitz Black-Eyed Susan (Fleuroselect Gold Medal First-Year-Flowering Rudbeckia)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-10 weeks before the last frost under bright light; sown early enough in long-day summer conditions, plants flower the same year rather than waiting until their second season like most seed-grown perennial rudbeckia.

directions: Start seed indoors in late winter and transplant into well-drained garden soil in full sun after the last frost, giving plants plenty of light to encourage first-year bloom. Goldblitz was bred to flower reliably in its first season from seed, closing the gap with vegetatively propagated black-eyed Susans like Goldsturm while needing a shorter daylength to initiate buds. Slightly smaller in leaf and flower than older seed strains, it still forms a tidy clump of golden, dark-coned daisies from midsummer into fall. Once established, divide crowded clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Zany Sunny-Side Up Gazania (Fleuroselect Gold Medal Compact Treasure Flower)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant after frost danger has passed, since gazania needs a long head start to bloom reliably its first season.

directions: Start seed indoors well ahead of the last frost and transplant into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, since gazania flowers close on cloudy or shaded days and need strong light to open fully. Zany Sunny-Side Up forms a tight, mounded rosette bred for pot and pack production, with daisy-like golden flowers held just above the silvery foliage on a plant barely eight inches tall. Its very uniform flowering window makes it dependable for edging and containers rather than mixed borders where taller companions might shade it out. Once established it tolerates heat and drought well, needing only occasional watering through summer.

common_name: Desire Red Sunflower (Fleuroselect Gold Medal Compact Branching Sunflower)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost in full sun once soil has warmed.

directions: Direct sow after the last frost in full sun, thinning seedlings so the compact, well-branched plants have room to spread without crowding. Desire Red carries wine-red petals around a deep burgundy center on short, sturdy stems that branch low on the plant, giving a single sunflower several blooms rather than one terminal flower. Standing just over two feet tall, it suits beds, borders, and containers better than taller single-stem sunflower types and needs no staking. Deadhead spent blooms to keep new side shoots flowering into fall.

common_name: Tiny Temptations F1 Orange Tomato (Fleuroselect Gold Medal Trailing Cherry Tomato)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into containers or baskets after frost danger has passed; this trailing type is bred for pots rather than staked garden rows.

directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into a hanging basket or large container in full sun once frost danger has passed, since Tiny Temptations grows as a petite trailing bush rather than an upright, staked vine. It produces an exceptionally heavy set of small, intensely sweet bright-orange cherry fruits over its small, sturdy green leaves, and the Fleuroselect jury singled it out for combining strong flavor with a tidy, self-contained habit that needs no pinching or staking. Its foliage shows good tolerance of common tomato diseases, keeping plants productive from early summer right through to frost. Harvest the fruit regularly, since they hold well on the plant without splitting or dropping.

common_name: Always Sunny Gold Sunflower (AAS and Fleuroselect Gold Medal Pollen-Free Sunflower)

planting.note: Direct sow in full sun after the last frost, giving plants plenty of room since this is a tall, vigorous, well-branched sunflower.

directions: Direct sow in full sun after the last frost, giving plants plenty of room since this is a tall, vigorous, well-branched sunflower rather than a compact bedding type. Always Sunny Gold opens velvet golden-yellow petals around a deep chocolate center on sturdy, highly branched stems that keep flowering for weeks longer than many comparison varieties, and because it produces no pollen it won't drop mess on patio furniture or trigger allergies. It earned recognition in both North American and European seed trials for its extended bloom and strong garden performance. Stake plants in exposed, windy sites and deadhead spent flowers to encourage continued branching.

common_name: Galactic White Compact Bacopa (Fleuroselect Gold Medal Seed-Grown Trailing Bacopa)

planting.note: Sow the fine seed uncovered indoors under bright light and transplant into baskets or borders after the last frost.

directions: Sow the fine seed uncovered indoors in moist mix under bright light, then transplant into hanging baskets, window boxes, or the front of borders after the last frost. Galactic White Compact was the first seed-grown bacopa to match the flower size of vegetatively propagated varieties, smothering its naturally branching, trailing mounds in small white flowers without needing pinching or growth regulators. It performs well in part sun to light shade, where it keeps blooming longer than in the hottest, driest exposures. Keep the shallow root mass evenly moist, since bacopa wilts quickly and recovers slowly if it dries out completely.

common_name: Heucherette Pink Coral Bells (Fleuroselect Gold Medal Seed-Grown Heuchera)

planting.note: Sow seed on the soil surface indoors, since Heuchera seed needs light to germinate; transplant young plants out in spring once well rooted.

directions: Sow seed uncovered under bright light indoors, since it needs light to germinate, then transplant into humus-rich, well-drained soil in light shade to morning sun once seedlings are established. Heucherette Pink is part of a compact, short-stemmed seed series bred to flower reliably from seed in its first year, pairing tidy mounded foliage with abundant pink flower spikes held just above the leaves. Unlike many heuchera grown from tissue-cultured divisions, it reaches a uniform, salable size quickly without special overwintering treatment. Give it consistent moisture and afternoon shade in hot climates, and divide congested clumps in spring every few years to keep them vigorous.

common_name: Flair Verbena (Fleuroselect Gold Medal Compact Tall Verbena)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost, since germination is naturally slow and uneven; transplant into lean, well-drained soil in full sun once frost danger has passed.

directions: Start seed indoors well ahead of the last frost, since germination is slow, then transplant into lean, well-drained soil in full sun once the weather has warmed. Flair is the most compact seed-grown Verbena bonariensis available, bred to stay genetically short and well-branched rather than tall and open like the wild species or older selections, so growers can skip pinching and growth regulators entirely. It still produces the same abundant clusters of small violet-purple flowers that draw butterflies and hummingbirds all summer, just on a tidier plant suited to containers and smaller borders. Once established it tolerates heat and dry spells with ease, needing only occasional watering through the season.

common_name: Estella Coral Salvia (Fleuroselect Gold Medal Early-Flowering Scarlet Sage)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into full sun once frost danger has passed.

directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into full sun once frost danger has passed, spacing plants about a foot apart for the looser, more elegant habit this series is known for. Estella Coral comes into bloom as much as two weeks earlier than standard scarlet sage, carrying soft coral-salmon flower spikes on taller, well-branched stems that suit large containers and border plantings better than stiffer bedding salvia types. It keeps flowering steadily through summer heat with only light grooming needed to remove spent spikes. Give it consistently moist, well-drained soil for the strongest color and longest bloom.

common_name: Corusco Cream-Red Coreopsis (Fleuroselect Gold Medal Compact Plains Coreopsis)

planting.note: Direct sow around the last frost in full sun, since plains coreopsis tolerates a light frost and germinates readily in cool soil.

directions: Direct sow around the last frost in full sun, since plains coreopsis tolerates a light frost and germinates readily in cool soil. Corusco Cream-Red was bred into an unusually compact, uniform mound without any need for growth regulators or pinching, covering itself in small cream-and-red bicolor daisies about ten weeks from sowing. Its tidy, even habit suits bedding and container use better than the taller, looser wild plains coreopsis it was selected from. It tolerates poor, dry soil and light neglect well, needing only minimal watering once established.

common_name: Masterpiece Blue with Eye Lobelia (Fleuroselect Gold Medal Bedding Lobelia)

planting.note: Start the fine seed indoors well ahead of the last frost, barely covering it, and transplant once nights stay reliably above freezing.

directions: Start the fine seed indoors well ahead of the last frost, barely covering it, and transplant into containers or bed edges once nights stay reliably above freezing. Masterpiece Blue with Eye smothers its low mound in small, vivid blue flowers each marked with a contrasting white eye, a crisp color combination that stands out from older solid-blue bedding lobelia. Like other Lobelia erinus, it performs best in cool to mild conditions and can stall or fade in prolonged summer heat, so afternoon shade helps extend its display in hot climates. Shear plants back lightly if they become sparse midseason to encourage a fresh flush of bloom.

common_name: Madonna Shasta Daisy (Fleuroselect Gold Medal First-Year-Flowering Shasta Daisy)

planting.note: Start seed indoors well ahead of the last frost and transplant into well-drained soil in full sun; sown early, plants flower their first season rather than waiting until year two.

directions: Start seed indoors well ahead of the last frost and transplant into well-drained soil in full sun; sown early enough, Madonna flowers reliably in its first season rather than waiting until its second year like most seed-grown shasta daisies. It forms a compact, uniform mound of white, yellow-centered daisies, with some blooms showing a lacy, fringed petal edge that sets it apart from plain-petaled shasta daisy types. Its even habit and strong vigor make it well suited to mass plantings and containers where consistent size matters. Deadhead spent flowers to extend bloom through summer, and divide established clumps every few years in spring to keep them vigorous.

common_name: Sibella Carmine Catchfly (Fleuroselect Gold Medal Nodding Catchfly)

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring or the previous fall in mild climates, since this cottage garden annual tolerates cool conditions well.

directions: Direct sow in early spring or the previous fall in mild climates, since this old-fashioned cottage garden annual tolerates cool conditions well and germinates best without summer heat. Sibella Carmine forms a low, wide-spreading mound smothered in small semi-double carmine-pink flowers, a tidier and more floriferous habit than older, looser nodding catchfly strains. Its compact, even growth suits edging, rock gardens, and mixed containers where a long season of small-scale color is wanted. Deadhead spent flowers regularly to prolong bloom, and expect the display to fade once summer heat sets in.

common_name: Baby Rose Nasturtium (Fleuroselect Gold Medal Dwarf Pink Nasturtium)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost in lean, well-drained soil, since rich soil pushes nasturtiums toward foliage over flowers.

directions: Direct sow after the last frost in lean, well-drained soil, since rich soil pushes nasturtiums toward foliage at the expense of flowers. Baby Rose forms a small, bushy clump of dwarf Tropaeolum minus, distinct from the more familiar trailing Tropaeolum majus nasturtiums, bearing bright pink-red flowers held above dark green foliage from early summer into fall. Its compact size suits pots, hanging baskets, and small border edges better than the sprawling vines of standard garden nasturtium. Keep watering light to moderate and avoid heavy feeding to keep the plant blooming heavily rather than growing lush leaves.

common_name: Sol Gekko Green Celosia (Fleuroselect Gold Medal Foliage Celosia)
scientific_name: Celosia argentea var. plumosa 'Sol Gekko Green'

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into full sun once the weather has warmed.

directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into full sun once the weather has warmed, since this is grown chiefly for its foliage rather than its small flower spikes. Sol Gekko Green opens with emerald-green leaves that deepen to a ruby-and-green bicolor after a week or two outdoors, accented by small hot-pink flower spikes, making it a distinctive foliage accent for borders and patio containers. It is bred to resist downy mildew, a common problem in older celosia foliage types, and finishes relatively quickly in production. Keep soil evenly moist through summer heat, and site it where its changing foliage color can be appreciated up close.

common_name: Amarillo Gold Rudbeckia (AAS and Fleuroselect Gold Medal Compact Black-Eyed Susan)

planting.note: Start seed indoors ahead of the last frost and transplant into full sun once frost danger has passed.

directions: Start seed indoors ahead of the last frost and transplant into full sun once frost danger has passed, giving plants room to form their compact, uniform mounds. Amarillo Gold flowers noticeably earlier than comparison black-eyed Susans and keeps blooming for weeks longer, covering its sturdy foot-tall plants in large, bright golden daisies with a light green center disc. Its even height and timing make it a reliable choice for mass bedding and containers where uniformity matters as much as color. It earned recognition in both North American and European seed trials for its extended, dependable bloom.

common_name: Gummy Bear Sunflower (Fleuroselect Gold Medal Double Pollen-Free Dwarf Sunflower)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost in full sun, thinning seedlings to allow the branching plants room to develop.

directions: Direct sow after the last frost in full sun, thinning seedlings to allow the branching, well-shaped plants room to develop. Gummy Bear produces fully double, fluffy, lemon-yellow blooms three to five inches across on a dwarf, uniform plant, a lighter-colored and slightly taller sibling to the similar Teddy Bear sunflower. Because the flowers produce minimal pollen, they are well suited to cutting and to gardeners who find standard sunflower pollen messy or irritating. Deadhead spent flowers to extend the mid-to-late-season bloom window, and stake in windy sites if needed.

common_name: Bellamy Blue Forget-Me-Not (Fleuroselect Gold Medal First-Year-Flowering Forget-Me-Not)

planting.note: Start seed indoors well ahead of the last frost; this variety blooms without a cold vernalization period, flowering in its first season.

directions: Start seed indoors well ahead of the last frost and transplant into consistently moist, humus-rich soil in light shade to morning sun once seedlings are sturdy. Bellamy Blue flowers without needing a cold vernalization period, so it blooms reliably in its first season rather than requiring fall sowing and overwintering like many forget-me-nots. It forms a dense, rounded ball of small, darker-blue flowers early on before loosening into a more spreading mound later in the season. Keep the soil from drying out, since this woodland-edge species wilts quickly in hot, dry conditions, and let a few flowers go to seed if self-sowing in a cottage border is wanted.

common_name: Belize Double Scarlet Zinnia (Fleuroselect Gold Medal Compact Double Zinnia)

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost in full sun, or set out transplants for earlier bloom.

directions: Direct sow after the last frost in full sun, or set out transplants for earlier bloom, since this zinnia's dense, mounded habit works well in both beds and containers. Belize Double Scarlet keeps its dome-like shape and strong branching from low on the plant without needing growth regulators, covering itself in fully double scarlet-red flowers through the growing season. Its compact, uniform habit distinguishes it from taller, looser zinnia types that tend to flop or need staking in exposed sites. Deadhead spent blooms regularly to keep new buds forming and extend color into fall.
